claim: The 'blue economy' includes deep-sea mining, offshore energy, underwater cables, high-seas fisheries and marine biotechnology.
source: Deep-sea mining, offshore energy, underwater cables, high-seas fisheries and marine biotechnology are just some sectors of the 'blue economy' (European Commission, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to European Commission, 2018

claim: The vast majority of deep-sea species have only recently been identified, and most remain undiscovered.
source: The vast majority of species have only recently been identified, and most remain undiscovered (Bouchet et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bouchet et al., 2016

claim: In 1978, riser pipes were used to recover approximately 800 tonnes of nodules from a depth of 5,500 m.
source: as far back as 1978, riser pipes were used to recover some 800 tonnes of nodules from the remarkable depth of 5,500 m (Nimmo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nimmo et al., 2013

claim: The Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) is a region of approximately six million km2 with typical depths of 4,000-5,500 m.
source: It is a region of approximately six million km2 with typical depths of 4,000-5,500 m and a sedimented, abyssal plain seafloor rich in polymetallic nodules
evidence: Direct statement about the physical characteristics of the CCZ

claim: Over 21 billion tonnes of nodules have been estimated to exist in the CCZ.
source: Over 21 billion tonnes of nodules have been estimated to exist in the CCZ; moreover, for nine metals critical to industry (including manganese, cobalt and nickel essential for modern green technologies such as battery-powered cars) the reserves in the CCZ nodules exceed the entire terrestrial reserve base (Hein et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hein et al., 2013

claim: For nine metals critical to industry, the reserves in the CCZ nodules exceed the entire terrestrial reserve base.
source: Over 21 billion tonnes of nodules have been estimated to exist in the CCZ; moreover, for nine metals critical to industry (including manganese, cobalt and nickel essential for modern green technologies such as battery-powered cars) the reserves in the CCZ nodules exceed the entire terrestrial reserve base (Hein et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hein et al., 2013

claim: As of July 2018, 16 exploration contracts with the ISA have been signed for nodule mining in the CCZ.
source: As of July 2018, 16 exploration contracts with the ISA have been signed for nodule mining in the CCZ, including five with European Union states (Germany, France, Belgium and two with the UK).
evidence: Direct statement of fact with specific date and number

claim: In recent years, between 10 and 20 exploration cruises have taken place every year to the CCZ.
source: In recent years, between 10 and 20 exploration cruises have taken place every year to the CCZ (ISA, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to ISA, 2015

claim: An extremely conservative estimate for the total number of research expeditions to the CCZ is at least 200.
source: An extremely conservative estimate for the total number of research expeditions to the CCZ is at least 200, considering that it has been actively explored for the last 40 years (Glover et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glover et al., 2015

claim: A five-degree box search in the shallow North Sea recovered over 80,000 annelid records of 1,500 taxa from the Ocean Biogeographic Information System.
source: For example, we searched for records of annelid worms (a dominant animal in both shallow and abyssal sedimented habitats) in a five-degree box (~300,000 km2) in the shallow North Sea, recovering over 80,000 records of 1,500 taxa.
evidence: Direct statement of search results, also shown in Figure 1a

claim: A five-degree box centered over the eastern CCZ recovers just nine annelid records from five taxa from the Ocean Biogeographic Information System.
source: However, a five-degree box centered over the eastern CCZ (the best-explored part of the CCZ) recovers just nine records from five taxa.
evidence: Direct statement of search results, also shown in Figure 1b

claim: Extending the search area to the entire CCZ recovers only three additional annelid records beyond the nine found in the eastern CCZ.
source: Remarkably, even extending the search area to the entire CCZ (~6,000,000 km2) still recovers only three additional records (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement of search results, also shown in Figure 1c

claim: The abyssal CCZ is one of the most biodiverse sedimented marine habitats on our planet.
source: It is not, and we know this from the few broad-scale studies of community ecology, which show that the abyssal CCZ is one of the most biodiverse sedimented marine habitats on our planet (Glover et al., 2002; Neal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glover et al., 2002 and Neal et al., 2011

claim: Abyssal plain annelid worm biodiversity is typically two to three times the diversity of shallow slope environments along continental margins.
source: Abyssal plain annelid worm biodiversity is typically two to three times the diversity of shallow slope environments along our continental margins (Neal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neal et al., 2011

claim: There has been almost no taxonomy done in the CCZ, and no systematic archiving of faunal data with accessible, vouchered and databased material in open, curated collections.
source: The reason for the lack of faunal lists of the CCZ is that there has been almost no taxonomy done, and no systematic archiving of faunal data with accessible, vouchered and databased material in open, curated collections.
evidence: Direct statement explaining the lack of taxonomic records

claim: Many hundreds of CCZ expeditions have taken place and perhaps tens of thousands of biological samples have been collected.
source: There has certainly been no lack of collecting effort; we know that many hundreds of CCZ expeditions have taken place and perhaps tens of thousands of biological samples have been collected (ISA, 2015; Glover et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to ISA, 2015 and Glover et al., 2015

claim: A typical 30-day expedition with 20 scientists and 20 crew to the CCZ on a modern research vessel would cost $1–2m, excluding the salary costs of the researchers.
source: A typical 30-day expedition with 20 scientists and 20 crew to the CCZ on a modern research vessel would cost $1–2m, depending on equipment used and excluding the salary costs of the researchers.
evidence: Direct statement of estimated expedition costs

claim: In recent years, almost all taxonomic studies in the CCZ that include full archiving of samples and genetic data have been funded by private contractors.
source: Interestingly, in recent years, almost all taxonomic studies in the CCZ that include full archiving of samples and genetic data have been funded by private contractors.
evidence: Direct statement about funding sources

claim: Recent taxonomic studies in the CCZ represent informal and formal descriptions of only 54 taxa, none of which are annelids.
source: Nevertheless, these studies represent informal and formal descriptions of only 54 taxa (none of which are annelids) out of perhaps several thousand left to describe.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Dahlgren et al., 2016; Glover et al., 2016; Wiklund et al., 2017; Gooday et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2017)

claim: The 'scaly-foot gastropod' was discovered at the hydrothermal vents of the deep Indian Ocean in 2001.
source: In 2001, a remarkable new species of animal called the 'scaly-foot gastropod' was discovered at the hydrothermal vents of the deep Indian Ocean (Warén et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warén et al., 2003

claim: Chrysomallon squamiferum is the only known metazoan to use iron in its skeleton.
source: the only known metazoan to use iron in its skeleton (Figure 2a).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2a

claim: The discovery and detailed taxonomic study of Chrysomallon squamiferum has opened up new knowledge on both the ecosystem value of hydrothermal vents and the challenges of management.
source: The discovery and detailed taxonomic study of this single animal has opened up a vast wealth of new knowledge on both the ecosystem value of hydrothermal vents and the challenges of management in an extraordinarily spatially-constrained and at-risk habitat (Chen et al., 2015a; Chen et al., 2015b; Chen et al., 2015c; Sigwart et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015a; Chen et al., 2015b; Chen et al., 2015c; Sigwart et al., 2017

claim: Plenaster craigi is probably the most common animal living on nodules in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone.
source: The small sponge Plenaster craigi is probably the most common animal living on nodules in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, and was only described in 2017 (Lim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2017 and shown in Figure 2b

claim: Plenaster craigi was only described in 2017.
source: The small sponge Plenaster craigi is probably the most common animal living on nodules in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, and was only described in 2017 (Lim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim et al., 2017

claim: Despite over 40 years of intensive sampling in the CCZ, the most abundant animal living on nodules had been completely overlooked.
source: Despite over 40 years of intensive sampling in the CCZ, the most abundant animal living on nodules had been completely overlooked.
evidence: Direct statement about the oversight of Plenaster craigi

claim: New microsatellite DNA data for Plenaster craigi demonstrate the potential value of a new protected area to the south of the mining zones.
source: In the case of P. craigi, new microsatellite DNA data demonstrate the potential value of a new protected area to the south of the mining zones (Taboada et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taboada et al., 2018

claim: In the period between June 2017 to June 2018, eight peer-reviewed papers on the taxonomy of CCZ animals were published.
source: For example, in the period between June 2017 to June 2018, eight peer-reviewed papers on the taxonomy of CCZ animals were published (Glover, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glover, 2018

claim: A target of 100 taxonomic descriptions per year for the CCZ could be relatively easily achieved with high-throughput, integrative DNA taxonomy approaches.
source: This could be relatively easily achieved with high-throughput, integrative DNA taxonomy approaches (Glover et al., 2015) and use of existing quality samples.
evidence: Supported by citation to Glover et al., 2015

claim: Major projects associated with a sustainable approach to deep-sea exploitation have been overly ecosystem-based.
source: To date, major projects associated with a sustainable approach to deep-sea exploitation have, in our opinion, been overly ecosystem-based (Pikitch et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pikitch et al., 2004 and stated as authors' opinion

claim: Sustainability and growth for the blue economy will only be achieved with an initial 'taxon-focused approach' to conservation.
source: We contend that sustainability and growth for the blue economy will only be achieved with an initial 'taxon-focused approach' to conservation.
evidence: Authors' contention based on their analysis

claim: It is not possible to model the ecosystem-wide impacts of deep-sea exploitation without any knowledge of the animals that live there.
source: We cannot, essentially, model the ecosystem-wide impacts of deep-sea exploitation without any knowledge of the animals that live there.
evidence: Logical inference from the lack of taxonomic knowledge

claim: Deep-sea mining has been severely constrained by a lack of basic scientific knowledge.
source: Deep-sea mining is an example of a major industrial activity that has been severely constrained by a lack of basic scientific knowledge, even though the cost of obtaining this information would be small relative to the potential size of the industry.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the constraints on deep-sea mining

claim: The cost of obtaining basic scientific knowledge would be small relative to the potential size of the deep-sea mining industry.
source: Deep-sea mining is an example of a major industrial activity that has been severely constrained by a lack of basic scientific knowledge, even though the cost of obtaining this information would be small relative to the potential size of the industry.
evidence: Authors' assessment of relative costs

claim: The engineering challenges of deep-sea mining are considerable, but not fundamentally a problem.
source: The engineering challenges are considerable, but not fundamentally a problem
evidence: Authors' assessment of engineering challenges

claim: UNCLOS and the ISA have put the brakes on deep-sea mining until a suitable legal, financial and environmental set of rules that are fair to all has been agreed.
source: Together, UNCLOS and the ISA have, commendably, put the brakes on deep-sea mining until a suitable legal, financial and environmental set of rules that are fair to all has been agreed.
evidence: Statement about the regulatory role of UNCLOS and ISA

claim: Polymetallic nodules are small potato-sized mineral accretions that sit on top of, or just slightly beneath, the sediment-water interface.
source: a sedimented, abyssal plain seafloor rich in polymetallic nodules – small potato-sized mineral accretions that sit on top of, or just slightly beneath, the sediment-water interface.
evidence: Direct description of polymetallic nodules

claim: Five European Union states have exploration contracts with the ISA for nodule mining in the CCZ: Germany, France, Belgium and two with the UK.
source: As of July 2018, 16 exploration contracts with the ISA have been signed for nodule mining in the CCZ, including five with European Union states (Germany, France, Belgium and two with the UK).
evidence: Direct statement of fact

claim: The lack of resources to complete post-expedition analysis and archiving of samples and data is the reason for the taxonomic failure on the high seas.
source: Almost certainly, the reason is the lack of resources to complete post-expedition analysis and archiving of samples and data.
evidence: Authors' inference about the cause of taxonomic failure

claim: A deep-sea expedition has a much higher relative cost compared to an inshore or terrestrial operation.
source: Typically, a deep-sea expedition has a much higher relative cost compared to an inshore or terrestrial operation.
evidence: General knowledge about expedition costs

claim: Taxonomic assessment is generally not seen as hypothesis-driven research, and can as such be lower-ranked than other projects.
source: Furthermore, taxonomic assessment is generally not seen as hypothesis-driven research, and can as such be lower-ranked than other projects (House of Lords, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to House of Lords, 2008

claim: Carl Linnaeus recognized in the 18th century that in order to make better use of biological diversity it was essential to systematize and standardize the naming system of species.
source: The father of modern taxonomic nomenclature – Carl Linnaeus – recognized in the 18th century that in order to make better use of biological diversity it was essential to systematize and standardize the naming system of species.
evidence: Historical knowledge about Linnaeus

claim: The modern obsession with the ecosystem-based approach to conservation does not translate well to the deep oceans where knowledge is poor.
source: However, the modern obsession with the ecosystem-based approach to conservation and sustainability – commendable in regions where we know the components of those ecosystems – does not translate well to the deep oceans where our knowledge is so poor.
evidence: Authors' assessment of conservation approaches

claim: Thurber et al. list carbon sequestration, methane oxidation, hydrocarbon extraction, deep-sea mining, deep-sea fisheries and many other examples of services provided by the deep seas.
source: For example, Thurber et al. list carbon sequestration, methane oxidation, hydrocarbon extraction, deep-sea mining, deep-sea fisheries and many other examples of services provided by the deep seas; they also make a noble attempt to list cultural benefits (such as inspiration and education) that are provided by research into the deep seas (Thurber et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thurber et al., 2014

claim: The ecosystem function of most deep-sea animals is completely unknown, as the animals themselves are undiscovered.
source: The truth is that the ecosystem function, let alone service, of most deep-sea animals is completely unknown, as the animals themselves are undiscovered.
evidence: Authors' statement about the state of knowledge

claim: In order to understand the functioning of, and services provided by deep-ocean ecosystems, we must study the integrative taxonomy and natural history of the animal components of that ecosystem.
source: We contend that in order to understand the functioning of, and services provided by our deep-ocean ecosystems, we must study the integrative taxonomy and natural history of the animal components of that ecosystem.
evidence: Authors' contention about necessary approach

claim: A fully integrative taxonomy that includes all available information on the biology and traits of new organisms coupled to archived specimens is a clear necessity for the study of ecosystem function and service.
source: A fully integrative taxonomy that includes all available information on the biology and traits of new organisms coupled to archived specimens is a clear necessity for the study of ecosystem function and service (Will et al., 2005; Wheeler, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Will et al., 2005 and Wheeler, 2018

claim: Chrysomallon squamiferum is formally known as the 'scaly-foot gastropod'.
source: Now formally known as Chrysomallon squamiferum (Chen et al., 2015a)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2015a

claim: It is hard to imagine how it would be possible to 'value' the Indian Ocean vent sites without knowledge of Chrysomallon squamiferum.
source: It is hard to imagine how it would be possible to 'value' the Indian Ocean vent sites without knowledge of this taxon – it is this iconic species that defines the vent in its scientific and public worth.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the importance of the species

claim: Plenaster craigi lives in the eastern Pacific abyssal plain, which is the largest continuous and open ecosystem on the planet.
source: Contrary to the constrained vent habitat of the scaly-foot gastropod, P. craigi lives in what must be the largest continuous and open ecosystem on the planet – the eastern Pacific abyssal plain.
evidence: Authors' characterization of the habitat

claim: Plenaster craigi is a slow-growing, widespread filter-feeding sponge.
source: As a slow-growing, widespread filter-feeding sponge with perhaps a rich microbiome with biotechnological spin-offs
evidence: Description of the species characteristics

claim: Plenaster craigi may have a rich microbiome with biotechnological spin-offs.
source: As a slow-growing, widespread filter-feeding sponge with perhaps a rich microbiome with biotechnological spin-offs
evidence: Speculative statement about potential microbiome

claim: Taxonomic knowledge that includes spectacular images or videos of deep-sea animals is invaluable in connecting broader society to the intrinsic value of wilderness regions.
source: And more broadly, taxonomic knowledge that includes spectacular images or videos of deep-sea animals is invaluable in connecting broader society to the intrinsic value of our wilderness regions.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the value of visual documentation

claim: The ISA has made commendable efforts to regulate industrial activity in the deep sea.
source: The ISA has made commendable efforts to regulate industrial activity in the deep sea, and in recent years, a raft of documents and recommendations has been produced, outlining both the process of gaining an exploitation contract (ISA, 2018) and a broader regional environmental management plan for some areas, including the CCZ (ISA, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to ISA, 2018 and ISA, 2011

claim: There has been an over-emphasis on a 'holistic' ecosystem approach to environmental data and ecosystem services in deep-sea regulation.
source: But we think that there has been an over-emphasis on a 'holistic' ecosystem approach to environmental data and ecosystem services, when what is most urgently needed are things as basic and fundamental as a list of the species that live in a contracted region, linked to archived samples and genetic material.
evidence: Authors' opinion about regulatory emphasis

claim: Information required for IUCN Red List assessment is lacking for the vast majority of the named deep-sea animals.
source: But information required for assessment is lacking for the vast majority of the named deep-sea animals, and those undescribed are not even eligible for evaluation.
evidence: Statement about the state of IUCN Red List data

claim: Undescribed deep-sea animals are not eligible for IUCN Red List evaluation.
source: But information required for assessment is lacking for the vast majority of the named deep-sea animals, and those undescribed are not even eligible for evaluation.
evidence: Statement about IUCN Red List eligibility requirements

claim: Deep-sea contractors are already funding some taxonomic work.
source: Deep-sea contractors are already funding some taxonomic work.
evidence: Direct statement of current practice

claim: 95 taxonomic papers on CCZ animals appeared in the period between June 2017 to June 2018.
source: For example, in the period between June 2017 to June 2018, eight peer-reviewed papers on the taxonomy of CCZ animals were published (Glover, 2018). These efforts should be recognized and encouraged by the ISA, and perhaps a minimum target set of 100 taxonomic descriptions per year (95 appeared in the period described above).
evidence: Inferred from the statement that 95 appeared in the period described, which refers to the June 2017 to June 2018 period

claim: A target of 100 taxonomic descriptions per year for the CCZ would mean that in ten years' time, 1,000 species from the CCZ would be described.
source: This would mean that in ten years' time (when some might quip that deep-sea mining will finally start), 1,000 species from the CCZ would be described.
evidence: Mathematical calculation based on proposed target

claim: With a modest funding boost shared jointly amongst contractors and stakeholders, 1,000 species descriptions could be delivered within five years.
source: With a very modest funding boost that could be shared jointly amongst contractors and stakeholders, this could easily be delivered within five years.
evidence: Authors' projection about achievable timeline

claim: Knowledge of a thousand new species would be a revolutionary leap in our understanding of the biodiversity, connectivity, community ecology, ecosystem function and services of the CCZ.
source: Knowledge of a thousand new species would be a revolutionary leap in our understanding of the biodiversity, connectivity, community ecology, ecosystem function and services of this vast region of our planet.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the impact of taxonomic knowledge

claim: A new emphasis on taxon-focused conservation may be the only way to develop the sustainable blue economy.
source: Globally, a new emphasis on taxon-focused conservation may be the only way to develop the sustainable blue economy that we all desire.
evidence: Authors' conclusion about conservation approach

claim: A five-year plan to deliver taxonomic and genomic knowledge on a thousand species in regions of the ocean earmarked for industrial activity is an achievable target.
source: For example, a five-year plan to deliver taxonomic and genomic knowledge on a thousand species in regions of the ocean earmarked for industrial activity is an achievable target.
evidence: Authors' assessment of feasibility stated in the abstract

claim: High-throughput, integrative taxonomy can provide the data that is needed to monitor various ecosystem services.
source: High-throughput, integrative taxonomy can, therefore, provide the data that is needed to monitor various ecosystem services (such as the natural history, connectivity, value and function of species) and to help break the regulatory deadlock of high-seas conservation.
evidence: Authors' claim about the utility of integrative taxonomy

claim: High-throughput, integrative taxonomy can help break the regulatory deadlock of high-seas conservation.
source: High-throughput, integrative taxonomy can, therefore, provide the data that is needed to monitor various ecosystem services (such as the natural history, connectivity, value and function of species) and to help break the regulatory deadlock of high-seas conservation.
evidence: Authors' claim about the utility of integrative taxonomy

claim: The shell length of Chrysomallon squamiferum is 4 cm.
source: Shell length 4 cm.
evidence: Direct measurement stated in Figure 2a caption

claim: The scale bar for Plenaster craigi in Figure 2b is 5 cm.
source: Scale bar 5 cm.
evidence: Direct measurement stated in Figure 2b caption
